The American frontier. Both a historical event and a literary mythology. It refers to the westward expansion of the United States from the eighteenth through twentieth centuries and to the cultural mythology surrounding it. In fiction and popular imagination, the frontier embodies individualism and courage and conflict and the taming of wilderness. These themes captivated American writers from Mark Twain to the present. The frontier myth has shaped American identity and literature as profoundly as any single concept.

Historically, the frontier marks the boundary between settled and unsettled territory, moving westward from the Atlantic coast. The U.S. Census officially declared it closed in eighteen ninety. In literature and culture, the frontier became a symbol of American exceptionalism and opportunity and the clash between civilization and nature. Mark Twain captured the frontier experience in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, setting them on the Mississippi River and immortalizing the freedom and moral complexity of frontier life.

The frontier archetype includes the self-made man and the outlaw and the lawman and the rancher and the prospector and the pioneer, all figures of American popular mythology. Associated with manifest destiny, the doctrine that American expansion across North America was inevitable and divinely ordained. Frontier narratives often elide or romanticize the displacement and genocide of Native Americans, making the myth a contested and problematic force in American letters. Western fiction and cattle-drive sagas and gold-rush stories draw on frontier mythology and remain central to American genre fiction.

The frontier persists in American consciousness and literature as a symbol of escape and reinvention and the allure of the open wilderness. Mark Twain was the writer who most powerfully captured frontier life and its moral implications. Western fiction is the literary genre most directly rooted in frontier mythology. Native Americans were the peoples whose displacement made frontier settlement possible, though they are often erased or vilified in frontier narratives. Individualism is the cultural value most closely associated with frontier mythology and character. Adventure fiction often overlaps with frontier narratives, employing templates of danger and discovery and survival.
